corrections.subject: The three approval rules were blanket prohibitions on the value alone, and the two approval coverage dimensions were literals; both replaced on 2026-10-04 by amendment APPROVAL-RULE-A1, which substitutes a six-element evidence requirement and computes both dimensions from the records
corrections.finding: Three governance rules in corpus.py failed validation on the VALUE of an approval field and nothing else. human_approval_rejected fired on any human_approval_status == 'approved', production_authorized_rejected on any production_authorized is True, verification_credit_rejected on any product_verification_credit is True; _validate_governance_semantics independently failed the same three fields as governance_authority_claim, so acceptance gate [7/8] failed on them too. Measured consequence: the corpus could not represent a legitimate approval at all. Its only reachable states for approval were absent and forbidden, a reviewer who had done the work had nowhere to record it, and the first signature would have turned `check` red and been blamed for it. The instrument was wrong rather than merely strict: a rule that fails on the value alone never inspects an approval, so it cannot distinguish a fabricated one from a real one and cannot say 'this one is unsigned'. Separately, the human_approval and production_authorization coverage dimensions were the literal {"numerator": 0}, with detail strings asserting 'all artifacts pending human approval (none performed)' and 'production_authorized=false for all artifacts (by policy)', and the coverage report's basis table classified both as 'constant'. A literal numerator reads 0/321 before any signature exists and would read 0/321 after three hundred, so neither dimension could distinguish 'no approvals' from 'not implemented', while its detail claimed a measured fact nothing had looked at. The third fault was in the instruction to reviewers: all 321 generated review packets told the reviewer holding the pen that recording their signature would turn `check` red, and that the human_approval dimension was a declared constant that would not move. Both statements described the prohibition rather than the rule, so a reviewer reading them would have been given confidently wrong instruction at the moment of signing.
corrections.decision: Both defects corrected, in the direction that changes no engineering content and adds no authority. DEFECT 1: the blanket prohibition is replaced by an EVIDENCE requirement read from role-and-review-policy.json#/approval_evidence_contract. An approval is NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT: it passes only if the record carries, under approval_evidence.<kind>, all six elements - the grant value; approved_by as a named individual rather than a role or a team; a declared role_id plus an independence object whose owner_role equals the record's own owner_role, with independence ENFORCED against both that owner role and the author of the last content revision; an ISO-8601 date grammar- and parse-checked; review_packet{path, sha256, record_sha256_at_signing} resolving to a packet.json on disk whose OWN integrity.record_sha256 equals the digest attested and whose target.record_id and target.profile name this record; and a revision_history entry recording the approval and citing the packet. Every finding names which element is unmet. production_authorization additionally requires an approving role holding production authority and a record family human approval is required for, so its bar is strictly higher rather than the same bar twice - both conditions reused from what the existing code and role-and-review-policy.json already distinguish, not invented. DEFECT 2: both dimensions are computed from the records by the SAME predicate the validator enforces, so neither can read higher than the gate permits. DEFECT 3: all 321 packets and all 321 packet.json twins were regenerated so the signature section states the rule actually in force - the six required elements, what the validator checks against each, and how to transcribe a correct approval - and `make_review_packets.py --transcribe ID` was added to print the pasteable block with both digests already resolved, writing nothing and filling no decision.

corrections.subject: CORR-COV-022 recorded four residual risks. Three are closed and one is reduced with the limit stated: approvals moved out of revision_history into an append-only ledger (RISK 4), staleness became a first-class measured state (RISK 3), reviews/signed/ became the ONLY admissible home for a signed packet (RISK 2), and forgery was made more costly and more detectable but is explicitly NOT prevented (RISK 1).
corrections.finding: CORR-COV-022 replaced a blanket prohibition with a six-element evidence requirement and recorded four residual risks rather than dropping them. Measured consequences of those four, all of which were real and all of which this correction addresses. RISK 4: element 6 of the contract required the approval to be recorded as a revision_history entry. A revision_history entry IS a content change, so recording an approval forced a revision bump; a bumped revision makes every link pinning that record's revision stale, and invalidates the sha256 that every review record stores for that record. So a properly evidenced approval could not be recorded without breaking two controls nobody had authorised breaking, and the corpus worked around it by recording the approval against the CURRENT revision - an unratified convention, open P3. The tell was the tool's own happy-path self-test, which had to select a record that NO review record covers, purely so the approval would not invalidate a review digest; a test that must choose an uncovered record to demonstrate its own happy path is demonstrating an unsatisfiable requirement, not a working one. RISK 3: the behaviour on a content change was correct - the approval stopped counting, because its attested digest no longer matched - but it was INVISIBLE. No finding, no count, no state. Only the numerator quietly stopped moving, which is indistinguishable from a reviewer who changed their mind. RISK 2: reviews/signed/ was an ordinary directory. Element 5 accepted a cited packet from either reviews/packets/ or reviews/signed/, and every packet told the reviewer to archive under signed/ as guidance rather than as a rule, so nothing stopped a reviewer citing the regenerated tree where the evidence would be destroyed by the next regeneration. RISK 1: a person can forge all six elements. That is irreducible.
corrections.decision: FOUR changes, in the direction that adds no authority and records nothing. RISK 4 CLOSED. Approvals moved out of revision_history into an append-only ledger, docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.jsonl. The record keeps only approval_ledger_ref, naming its ledger entry. The mechanism that makes this free is a CONTENT DIGEST: the content digest of a record is its bytes projected through a view in which approval evidence is removed and approval state is reset to the no-claim values every record already carries. A neutral record therefore projects to its own bytes - which is why all 261 stored review digests still verify unchanged - and an approved record projects back to the file it had before the approval, rendered in that file's own DETECTED layout (the 321 records are a mix of 1- and 2-space indent, so the layout is probed and verified rather than assumed). The review-digest check compares the content digest. So recording an approval neither bumps the revision, nor stales a link, nor invalidates a review digest, and a self-test performs the whole recording on a throwaway copy of a COVERED record and asserts all three. RISK 3 CLOSED. An entry whose approved_record_sha256 no longer matches is STALE, which is explicitly NOT invalid: it does not fail validation, it is counted in a new approval_staleness metric as stale/total, and it is reported in a finding naming the record, the ledger entry and the fields that changed - recoverable because every signed packet embeds the approved record verbatim under record_verbatim, so the validator diffs approved bytes against current bytes instead of printing two opaque digests. A stale approval is excluded from the human_approval numerator, because that numerator means 'records carrying an approval that describes the bytes now on disk'; it is not discarded, because human_approval and approval_staleness together account for every approval. RISK 2 CLOSED. A cited packet is admissible ONLY from docs/artifacts/reviews/signed/. A citation into docs/artifacts/reviews/packets/ is rejected with a message that says the signed packet must be archived first, because a reviewer told only that their path is wrong will look for a different wrong path. RISK 1 REDUCED, NOT FIXED, and the residual limit is recorded in three places - the corpus-policy amendment, docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.md, and the checker itself - in the same words: the hash chain proves existence, ordering and integrity; the git anchor proves when and in what state the packet was committed; neither proves that a human read anything, and none of this makes an approval unforgeable. That limit is irreducible. Three things raise the COST of forgery and make it DETECTABLE: each entry binds to its predecessor's digest, so deleting, reordering or editing any entry breaks the chain from that point on and the validator reports the FIRST break; each entry cites the git commit that first contained the signed packet, and the validator confirms that commit exists and holds the blob; and the archive rule is now a rule. None of the three is prevention.

corrections.subject: Two governance items left open by CORR-COV-022 and CORR-COV-023 are DECIDED, and neither moves a coverage dimension. (1) human_approval_status 'not_required' was an open P3 and is now answered on the merits: it is a LEGITIMATE value, permitted only on a record family that genuinely does not require approval, and never counted toward the human_approval numerator. (2) An approval now requires TWO signatures - an approver and an independent countersigner - which raises the cost and changes the shape of forgery without preventing it, and is accounted for layer by layer in a new forge_resistance report.
corrections.finding: ITEM 1. 'not_required' had been carried as an open P3 through two amendments. Mechanically it was a grant by the same test that treats 'approved' and 'rejected' as grants (any value other than 'pending'), so it was rejected by human_approval_rejected at elements 1-6 for want of an approval_evidence block it could not have. The verdict was COHERENT and reached for the WRONG REASON: it is correct that a record declaring no approval gate must not smuggle an approval past the evidence contract, but the value was never examined to decide whether it was legitimate at all. On the tree this corpus ships, 'pending' was the ONLY value of human_approval_status that was both schema-valid and validator-valid - 'not_required' was already in the enum in artifact-base.schema.json and already listed in role-and-review-policy.json#/approval_semantics/human_approval_status_values, so the schema permitted it and the validator rejected it, which is an inconsistency in the corpus rather than a policy choice. Two genuinely different states were indistinguishable: a record on a family with no sign-off gate, and a record waiting for an approval that will never come. Both read 'pending'. Meanwhile review_policy.additional_fields/human_approval_required_for is a POSITIVE LIST of three families, so the scoping the policy declares could be enforced negatively and never recorded positively. ITEM 2. The approval contract's six elements, the hash chain and the git anchor all bind ONE signature, and a single binding is satisfied by a single forger. Every layer therefore detected tampering with the RECORD while none of them prevented one determined person writing a self-consistent ledger entry, a real packet and a real commit - which is what the independent checker's own output has always said. CORR-COV-023 recorded that as RISK 1 and reduced it without closing it, correctly, but RISK 1 was reduced by adding cost to a forgery that still required only ONE person.
corrections.decision: ITEM 1, DECIDED: LEGITIMATE, PERMITTED ONLY WHERE APPROVAL IS NOT REQUIRED, NEVER COUNTED TOWARD THE human_approval NUMERATOR. 'not_required' stops being a grant: APPROVAL_RULES['human_approval'] gains non_grant_values, _is_approval_grant honours it, and the value is therefore never 'granted', never 'evidenced' and never 'evidenced_now'. The six-element contract is not reached for it at all, which is correct - there is no approval to evidence. The boundary is the policy's own positive list, READ rather than restated: 'not_required' is permitted on any record whose artifact_type is not in approval_evidence_contract/production_authorizable_artifact_types/types, which is {safety_case, post_development_record, change} on this corpus. On those three families it is REJECTED, at high severity, by the new rule id human_approval_not_required_misdeclared, reached by BOTH _validate_artifact and _validate_governance_semantics so gate [7/8] cannot be blind to it. Two contradictions are rejected too: a 'not_required' record carrying an approval_evidence.human_approval block, and one carrying an approval_ledger_ref resolving to a human_approval ledger entry. The DENOMINATOR is unchanged at every record carrying an id, so relabelling cannot remove a record from the measurement, and the count is reported inside the human_approval dimension - in its detail text and as the machine-readable fields not_required_records and not_required_misdeclared - so relabelling moves a number that is on the record rather than one that is quietly absent. It is NOT a review exemption: automated_review_coverage counts such a record exactly like any other. ITEM 2, DECIDED: AN APPROVAL REQUIRES TWO SIGNATURES. Element 7 adds a countersignature nested inside approval_evidence.<kind>, carrying the countersigner's own full six-element evidence over the SAME packet digest, and the ledger entry carries the same object - so the hash chain binds both signatures TOGETHER rather than binding two chains. Two entries would have let a forger drop the countersignature and leave the chain valid, which is precisely the property the second signature exists to remove. Seven clauses are checked separately so a rejection names which failed: a declared role_id; not the record's owner_role; not the author of ANY content revision at or below the revision being approved (a STRICTER test than the approver faces, which excludes only the last content author, and one that genuinely differs here because 36 records carry two or three content authors); not the approver's role; not a role the policy excludes for that record's owner_role; a name that shares no token with the approver's, compared on normalised token sets so 'Ada Lovelace' and 'A. Lovelace' are one person; and a person rather than a role or a team. The per-owner_role exclusion map is declared in the policy and READ by the code, not inferred by it. Eight owner_role values on disk are not declared in roles[] at all, so for those records the per-owner_role clause has an empty exclusion set; that is recorded as a DECLARED GAP in the policy rather than closed by inventing role definitions, which is the same refusal CORR-COV-021 recorded. The residual limit is stated in four places and nowhere is any layer described as preventing forgery.

corrections.why_this_is_not_a_weakening: Stated rather than asserted, because both items are exactly the kind of change that should be distrusted. FOR ITEM 1: (a) it is not a relaxation of any existing control - every record the previous rules caught is still caught, and the only new reachable state is one that previously had no representation at all; (b) the value cannot raise the numerator, and that is measured through the dimension's OWN counting function rather than by observing that the numerator is 0 on a corpus with no approvals anyway; (c) the relaxation is bounded by the policy's own positive list, so the evasion a reader should worry about - relabelling a pending record to dodge a future approval - is rejected on exactly the families where an approval could ever be owed; (d) the denominator is unchanged, so relabelling cannot shrink the population being measured; (e) the value is not a review exemption, and automated_review_coverage is deliberately untouched so that a not_required record with no review stays a visible gap; (f) five self-tests prove it in BOTH directions, including rejection across all three required families rather than one, and including parity between _validate_artifact and _validate_governance_semantics. FOR ITEM 2: (a) every approval that was valid before is still valid, because the existing fixture builder now supplies a well-formed countersignature and the happy path test is unchanged and still passes; (b) every single-signature approval that would previously have been ACCEPTED is now REJECTED, so the change can only turn an acceptance into a rejection and never the reverse; (c) a test asserts a properly countersigned approval on a record a review record ALREADY COVERS is accepted and does not stale that review digest, which is the failure mode CORR-COV-022 found in the old element 6; (d) a test measures over all 321 records that at least two independent signing parties remain available for every one - worst case 6 eligible countersigner roles - because a two-party rule that made approval impossible for some record type would be a functional regression disguised as a control; (e) the countersignature role in the fixture is CHOSEN BY ASKING THE TOOL rather than hard-coded, so the tests cannot silently start failing when the policy map changes; (f) nothing existing was removed: the chain, the anchor, the archive rule, elements 1-6, the independence rule and the production-authority bar are all untouched, and the self-tests asserting the ones that could plausibly have been affected still pass; (g) a test asserts the forge_resistance report exists, enumerates all six layers, states each layer's limit, and contains no sentence asserting rather than denying that any layer prevents forgery.
corrections.residual_risks_recorded_here_not_silentl: FOUR, none closed by this correction and two of them newly introduced by it. (1) FORGERY IS NOT PREVENTED AND IS NOT CLAIMED TO BE. One forger acting alone is no longer enough - a forgery now requires two people to be named, to hold roles independent of the record's owner_role and of every content author, to attest the same packet digest, and to appear in one entry whose chain stays intact. TWO COLLUDING PARTIES ARE STILL ENOUGH, and they may collude trivially by one person writing two names in two role-shaped forms. The name comparison is token-set based, so 'Ada Lovelace' and 'A. Lovelace' are correctly rejected as one person, but a second INVENTED name in a different shape is indistinguishable from a second real person and nothing here can tell them apart. AND NO NUMBER OF SIGNATURES FIXES IT: a third needs three colluding parties and the residual does not approach zero with arity. The limit is that ATTESTATION IS NOT PROOF OF COMPREHENSION, and it is irreducible. Recorded in four places - corpus-policy.json review_policy.approval_countersignature_contract.residual_limit_that_this_does_not_reduce (for the countersignature), approval-ledger.md#forge_resistance, closing-list.md 0.2f, and the acceptance gate's own residual line - and a self-test asserts the wording is present and that no text asserts rather than denies unforgeability. (2) OPEN P2, UNCHANGED: eight undeclared owner_role values (change_manager, configuration_manager, cybersecurity_engineer, data_quality_engineer, integration_engineer, quality_engineer, sys_engineer, verification_lead) are still not in role-and-review-policy.json#/roles. That now has a SECOND consequence beyond the one recorded at 1.6: the countersigner's per-owner_role exclusion map has no entry for those roles either, so a countersignature on a record they own is checked STRICTLY LESS than on a record owned by a declared role. The gap is declared in the policy's unmapped_owner_role_policy rather than closed by inventing role definitions. Adding those roles to roles[] and to the map is the follow-up and it is the highest-value open item. NOTE the earlier figure of seven undeclared owner_role values recorded in closing-list.md 1.6 is wrong; measured, it is eight. (3) A QUIET FAILURE MODE NO RULE DETECTS: 'not_required' is one keystroke from 'pending', and a record that NEEDED a sign-off and says 'pending' forever is indistinguishable from one that is simply not due yet. A record that needed a gate and says 'not_required' IS caught, by the new rule. The silent case is not. (4) BOTH NEW ITEMS ARE UNEXERCISED BY THE LIVE TREE: 0 of 321 records carry 'not_required', so the decision is about representability and the self-tests are the only evidence it works; and the ledger holds 0 entries, so element 7 is likewise only exercised by self-tests. Those are tests of the rule, not of any approval.

corrections.subject: verification_planning's 33/7 is not a coverage ratio and never was; the basis is now stated in the dimension's own detail string and in machine-readable fields beside it. Also recorded here: the machine control that now reads the behaviours[] layer of every implementation record, the four-way split of verified_against_pinned_source, the defect class that control exposed in the source registry, and the decision to mark reports/coverage-report.md archival rather than re-baseline it.
corrections.finding: ITEM 1 - verification_planning. The dimension put the count of records whose id carries -TMS- in the numerator and the count of records whose id carries -FSR- in the denominator. Those are disjoint populations: a test measure is not a safety requirement. The detail string read '33 test measures for 7 FSRs', which a reader parses as 4.7 measures per requirement, and the dimension's own description said 'test measures per safety requirement; a ratio, not a score, and over 100% means over-covered' - a statement that is false of these two numbers. No artefact said what the ratio was meant to measure, and no self-test pinned the meaning, so the ratio could have changed meaning without anything detecting it. MEASURED from the link registry: 7 of 7 safety requirements have at least one test measure linked to them (as_is 3/3, synthetic_reference 4/4) and 9 of 33 test measures verify at least one safety requirement (as_is 3/5, synthetic_reference 6/28). So the answer to the question the ratio appears to ask is 7/7, and the ratio as published cannot express it. ITEM 2 - the behaviours layer had no machine control at all: 84 behaviours across 14 implementation records cite an evidence_symbol and an evidence_line_range and no file, and no rule in the suite read behaviours[]. Three provenance rules now read it (behaviour_citation_unresolved, behaviour_citation_line_range_out_of_bounds, behaviour_citation_symbol_missing) and the implementation schema declares the resolution contract. Of the 84, 68 resolve to a code_location at exactly the cited range, 16 to one whose range contains it, and 1 resolved to nothing and was repaired. ITEM 3 - verified_against_pinned_source was one boolean over four checks; all 82 code_locations now carry the four parts by name and both the aggregate and each part are machine-checked. ITEM 4 - reading pinned blobs rather than the working tree exposed a defect the corpus's only provenance reader cannot see: 13 of the 117 source anchors with a usable content_hash record a hash that is not the sha256 of the blob at the commit the same anchor names, while all 13 match the checked-out file. Recorded as FB2-REV-FND-000197.
corrections.decision: ITEM 1: the ratio is RETAINED at 33/7 and is not redefined, because a dimension whose meaning changes when it is tidied cannot be compared with any earlier run of itself. What changed is that the detail string now says in words what each number counts, that it states the measured 7/7 and 9/33 beside them, and that four machine-readable fields (test_measure_records, safety_requirement_records, requirements_with_a_linked_measure, measures_verifying_a_requirement) and a ratio_is_a_coverage_ratio flag carry the same facts without prose. The dimension's description was corrected to stop calling it measures per safety requirement. ITEM 2: the second option in FB2-REV-FND-000172's disposition was taken - declare that behaviour evidence resolves against the record's own code_locations and machine-check it - rather than adding a file to 84 behaviours, because resolution against a located symbol whose pinned blob is re-derived is a verification and a path field is an assertion. ITEM 3: the field was split AND both the aggregate and each part were made machine-checked; a rename would have left four checks behind a name, and a split alone would have left four asserted booleans in place of one. ITEM 4: referred, not repaired - see FB2-REV-FND-000197. coverage-report.md is marked ARCHIVAL: it is a dated snapshot of the 2026-10-01 run whose value is its audit trail, so re-baselining it would have destroyed the trail it exists to preserve and re-created the staleness immediately, and leaving it readable as current is the one option that is not available.
